The day — moment 2 of 3 · the plan forming as they talk
The day — moment 3 of 3 · it asks whether to send
The kitchen card — a sheet off the day, in Hindi

annotations.text: Moments 1-3 are ONE screen at three points in the same Thursday afternoon, not three screens. What is fixed is the ORDER — wordmark, date, day card, the one-line remark, the talk bar — not the heights: the day card grows and shrinks with what is in it, so an undecided dinner is a one-line row and a decided one opens into two menus. There is no navigation anywhere in the app: if it can be spoken, it is not a destination.

The day never scrolls. The talk scrolls underneath it, so the menu he is building stays in front of him while he speaks. The two columns carry the information structurally: a dish that is the same for everyone spans the full width (curd, papad), a dish that differs splits into two (khichdi, banded in amber — one pot, Krishna's portion out before the mirchi). The steel-tinted row is what his last exchange added; it fades.

Nothing is settled until he says so out loud, and the system asks for that agreement explicitly, so a loose "that's fine" cannot be mistaken for it. The plan card's border turns steel once it has converged and stopped changing. No send button lives here — it is on the sheet, after he says yes.

The only thing that leaves the conversation, and so the only thing that earns a screen of its own: a different reader, a different language. Two outputs — the menu as a card, and the same menu written out as prose for whoever is cooking it. It exists only once he has agreed.
